lesson.title: When the Numbers Lie: The Craft of Numerical Limit Estimation
lesson.summary: Tables of values are a powerful first step toward guessing a limit, but knowing their blind spots, rounding error and rapid oscillation, is what keeps a numerical estimate from becoming a wrong answer.
lesson.body:
Building on limits-from-tables, numerical estimation is the broader skill of using computed values to responsibly guess a limit: choosing which x-values to test, how many decimal places to trust, and recognizing the warning signs that an apparently clean pattern is not actually the real answer.

Precision matters more than it first appears. A calculator or a rounded display can make tiny, meaningful differences between consecutive table rows disappear, or it can make ordinary rounding noise look like a real trend. Computing a couple of extra rows on each side of the target x-value, and carrying enough decimal places to see genuine movement in the output, builds real confidence that a numeric pattern reflects the function and not just rounding. As a rule of thumb, each new row should be roughly ten times closer to the target x-value than the last, so any genuine limiting trend has room to reveal itself clearly across the table.

The clearest cautionary example is lim as x approaches 0 of sin(1/x). Suppose a table is built using x-values of the convenient form x = 1/(n times pi) for whole numbers n, say n = 10, 100, 1000, giving x approximately 0.0318, 0.00318, 0.000318. For every one of these, 1/x equals n times pi exactly, and sin(n times pi) equals 0 for every whole number n, so every single row of this table reads exactly 0, seemingly showing the limit is 0 with perfect consistency. But this consistency is an illusion created by a very special choice of x-values. Testing a different, equally reasonable sequence instead, x = 1/[(2n + 0.5) times pi], gives 1/x = (2n + 0.5) times pi, and sin of that expression works out to exactly 1 for every single value of n, a table that instead suggests the limit is 1. Two carefully constructed tables, both using x-values marching steadily toward 0, giving two completely different constant outputs, is unmistakable evidence that sin(1/x) is actually oscillating infinitely often between -1 and 1 as x approaches 0, and that the limit simply does not exist.

The general lesson: a numerical estimate deserves real trust only when many different, independently chosen sequences of x-values approaching a from both sides all agree on the same output trend. If the apparent answer changes depending on exactly which x-values were tested, that is strong evidence the limit does not exist, most often because of oscillation, rather than evidence that any one of the competing answers is correct.

As a practical habit, pair every numerical estimate with an independent check whenever one is available, an algebraic simplification as in the algebraic limit technique or complex fractions chapters, or a graph as in limits-from-graphs. Treat a table as a way to generate a hypothesis worth testing further, not as a proof by itself, and be especially cautious with trigonometric, periodic, or otherwise oscillatory expressions, where a table can look perfectly convergent while the true behavior nearby is anything but.
